passage:
Hostel warden's note, girls' wing, Term 2
Gurleen, Class 11, has been handing in homework late for three weeks. Her roommate Elizabeth told me Gurleen watches short videos on her phone until two or three most nights and then sleeps through the morning bell.
I spoke with Gurleen on Thursday. She was defensive at first, then admitted, "I open it for five minutes and look up and it's midnight." She seemed tired and fed up with herself.
We agreed on a small plan she chose herself: phone charges at the warden's desk from eleven, alarm clock instead of phone alarm, and one hour of video on Sundays as a treat.
Elizabeth offered to study with her after dinner.
I have informed her parents and will check in with her every Monday for a month.

qa.q: Where will Gurleen's phone charge from eleven?
qa.a: At the warden's desk.

qa.q: How did Gurleen feel when she admitted how long she spent on videos?
qa.a: She felt tired and fed up with herself, after being defensive at first.

qa.q: What makes the warden's plan likely to work?
qa.a: Gurleen chose the steps herself, the plan is small and clear, and there are weekly check-ins and a study partner.

qa.q: How is Elizabeth affected by Gurleen's late nights?
qa.a: As a roommate, Elizabeth sees the problem up close and cares enough to offer to study together after dinner.

grounding: A warden's note on a teen struggling with late-night screen use and building a simple discipline plan.

passage:
Tuesday night
Neelam's older cousin offered us a vape behind the tuition centre today. Neelam took it. Everyone was watching me.
I said no. Well, I said, "Nah, my asthma," which is half true. My heart was going crazy. Nobody pushed, but a boy laughed.
On the walk home Neelam said, "It's just flavour, it's harmless." I don't think that's true, we literally did a chapter on it. But I didn't argue. I didn't want to sound like a teacher.
I told Mumma at dinner, without naming Neelam's cousin at first. She didn't shout. She thanked me, and we agreed she'd have a word with the tuition centre about who hangs around behind it.
I'm glad I said no. I'm worried about Neelam.
Sarita

qa.a: Behind the tuition centre.

qa.q: What was Sarita feeling when everyone was watching?
qa.a: Sarita felt nervous and pressured; the heart was going crazy.

qa.q: Which choice worked, and what could Sarita do about Neelam?
qa.a: Saying no and telling Mumma the same day worked; Sarita can also talk to Neelam privately or ask a trusted adult to help.

qa.q: How might Neelam feel if Sarita raised it gently?
qa.a: Neelam may feel defensive at first but perhaps also relieved that a friend cares.

Class teacher's note, Class 10-A, civics project
For the unit on local government, Joseph and Nazia chose to track how complaints reach the municipal office. They filed a real complaint about a broken streetlight near school and followed it.
Joseph was frustrated when nothing happened for two weeks. He wanted to post angry comments online. Nazia said her father would be upset if the family name appeared in a public fight.
They argued, then chose a middle path: a polite follow-up letter, signed by both families, and a visit to the ward office. The light was fixed in the fourth week.
In their presentation, Joseph said, "I thought respecting rules meant staying quiet. It means using them properly." I have shared their letter as a model with the other sections.

qa.a: A broken streetlight near school.

qa.a: He felt frustrated and impatient, wanting to post angry comments online.

qa.q: How might Nazia's father see the way they handled it?
qa.a: He would likely feel relieved and proud that the complaint was made respectfully without a public fight.

grounding: A teacher records teens balancing civic action with care for family reputation.

Big fight with Papa today. Our cousin's wedding is next month, and Papa wants the band to play on the road till midnight. I said there's a noise rule after ten, and I read it's the law.
He said, "The whole family will laugh at us if the baraat is quiet."

Joseph came to me on Wednesday with a screenshot. A group chat had been sharing an edited photo of Rukmini with a mean caption. Joseph had been added to the chat and felt sick seeing it.
He told me he had not forwarded it. He had written in the group, "This is not okay, delete it," and then left. Two boys had called him a traitor.

I will check on both Rukmini and Joseph next week.

Hostel mentor's note, first-year students, October
Sharmila came to see me after her phone was cut off for an unpaid bill. It was her first time handling money without her parents; they send an amount at the start of each month.
She showed me her spending. Most of it went in the first ten days on food delivery and a trip with friends. She was embarrassed and near tears. "At home I never even saw the bills."
Her roommate Bidisha, who works part-time, showed her how she writes every expense in a notebook each night.
I did not tell Sharmila what to spend. I suggested she list her fixed bills first and talk to the college's student finance advisor, who runs free sessions.
She booked one for Monday.

The water pump in Rajni's rented room broke on the same day her exams started. Her landlord was out of town. Her roommate Zeenat had gone home for a wedding.
Rajni stood in the tiny kitchen with a sink full of dishes and no running water, and felt like sitting on the floor.
Instead she made a list. Fill buckets from the society tap downstairs. Wash only what she needed. Hand-wash two sets of clothes. Cook one pot of khichdi to last two days.

By night she had clean plates, clean clothes and revision notes open. The caretaker fixed the pump the next afternoon. Rajni ate khichdi and felt, for once, like a grown-up.

The free hours disappeared. I'd plan to study after lunch, then scroll, nap, chat, and suddenly it was dinner. By October I was behind in two subjects and panicking every night.

I still waste time. Less now. And I've stopped laughing at planners.

passage:
Workshop supervisor's note, welding apprentices
Kashish joined our six-month welding course in March with a B.Com degree. The other apprentices teased her that she'd leave in a week.
She didn't. In the first month her welds were uneven and she burned her glove twice. I noticed she stayed after hours practising on scrap metal, and asked Pooja, our senior welder, to watch her.
Pooja taught her how to hold a steady hand by resting her elbow. By the third month Kashish's welds passed inspection.
She told me, "My degree taught me to think. This teaches me to do."

At the college career fair, held in the badminton hall, Darshan stood by the architecture firm stalls with a folder of printed drawings, too shy to walk up.
Ritu, from his batch, came over. "You've been standing here for twenty minutes."
"They look busy."
"They're here to talk to us." She nudged him. "Ask one question. That's it."
He went to the smallest stall. "Excuse me, what do interns actually do at your firm?"
The architect laughed. "Mostly make models and coffee. Want to see?" She showed him photos, looked at his drawings, and gave him her card. "Email me in January."
Darshan walked back to Ritu, card clutched, legs shaking. "I have to write an email now."
"Yes. Tonight, while you're brave."

qa.a: In the badminton hall.

qa.q: What was Darshan feeling while standing by the stalls?
qa.a: He felt shy and nervous, too scared to walk up for twenty minutes.

qa.a: It broke the task into one question, which made it possible for Darshan to start a real conversation.

qa.q: How might the architect see Darshan's question?
qa.a: She seemed to find it honest and friendly, which is why she laughed, looked at his drawings and gave him her card.

Okay, Vijay, you asked how I got the internship at the publishing house. Honestly, it started with a mistake.
I'm Bhavna. In second year I emailed ten companies a copy-pasted letter. Nobody replied. I felt invisible.
Then my professor said, "People help people they've met." So I went to every book launch in the city for three months. I stood at the back, nervous, holding a cold samosa. I asked one editor one question each time.
One of them, an older man who ran a small press, remembered me by the fourth launch. He said, "You again. What do you actually want?"
I told him. He gave me a two-week trial proofreading. I worked like mad.
That trial became a summer internship.

In a shared kitchen in Seoul, Soo-ah stared at two things on the table: her biology notes on how leaves repel water, and a stack of cheap umbrellas that had leaked on the way home.
Her flatmate Esther, a design student from Ghana, picked up a leaf from the window plant and dripped water on it. "It just rolls off."
"Tiny bumps," Soo-ah said. "And wax. What if fabric copied that?"
They spent the night sketching. Esther drew shapes; Soo-ah looked up coatings. By morning they had a messy idea for a raincoat fabric patterned on a lotus leaf.
It probably wouldn't work the first time. Soo-ah didn't care. She felt more awake than she had all semester, the two subjects clicking together like puzzle pieces.

qa.a: How leaves repel water.

qa.q: How did Soo-ah feel by morning?
qa.a: She felt energised and excited, more awake than all semester.

qa.q: What could Soo-ah and Esther do next to test their idea?
qa.a: They could make a small sample and ask a teacher in each department for feedback before going further.

qa.a: Esther's design skill gets a new purpose, and she seems equally caught up in the idea.

The community centre's innovation challenge had one rule: solve a problem in your own neighbourhood. Gargi, a music student, and Hansa, a computer science student, were paired almost by accident.
Hansa wanted an app. Gargi wanted a song. They argued for two days.
Then Gargi mentioned that her grandmother kept missing her medicines because she couldn't read the small labels. Hansa went still. "What if the pillbox plays a different tune for each medicine?"
Gargi was already humming. They built it from a cheap speaker and a small circuit board: a morning raga, an afternoon folk tune, an evening lullaby.
The judges asked where the idea came from. Gargi said, "From two people who didn't want to work together."

qa.a: A different medicine: a morning raga, an afternoon folk tune, an evening lullaby.

qa.a: Hansa felt struck and suddenly curious, going still as the idea formed.

qa.q: What went wrong at first, and what turned it around?
qa.a: They argued over an app versus a song; a real problem from Gargi's family let them join both skills.

qa.q: How might Gargi's grandmother feel using the pillbox?
qa.a: She might feel relieved and more independent, recognising each medicine by its tune.

grounding: Shows young adults from different fields combining ideas into an original product.

Dear Tanuja didi,
You always said I think in strange directions. Here's proof.
I'm studying economics but I spend my weekends at the farmers' market with Chacha. I noticed farmers throw away bruised tomatoes, while the chaat stalls buy expensive puree.
So I did something odd: I used what I learned in my supply chain class and what Chacha knows about ripening, and I made a plan to connect the two. The farmers sell bruised tomatoes cheap at noon, the stalls get them fresh.

I'm going to refine it. I've never felt so excited about economics.
Pradeep
